title: Astronaut Photographs a Patch of 'Moon Rock' on Earth
summary:
When you look up at the Moon, you can see bright, light-colored areas called the highlands. Much of that brightness comes from a rock called anorthosite. Now an astronaut has photographed a giant patch of the same kind of rock right here on Earth.

On August 28, 2026, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station took a picture of the Saririaky anorthosite massif in southern Madagascar, an island country off the east coast of Africa. A massif is a large body of rock. Seen from space, this one forms a bright, roughly circular shape that stands out against the dry land around it. It covers about 100 square kilometers, or 40 square miles.

Anorthosite is an igneous rock, which means it forms from melted rock that cools and hardens. This type forms underground, where it cools slowly. That slow cooling gives its minerals time to grow into fairly large crystals. Besides Madagascar, big deposits are also found in eastern Canada, Scandinavia and southern India.

Scientists think the Saririaky rock formed at least 600 million years ago. The rocks around it tell an exciting story, too. Long ago, pieces of land crashed together to form Gondwana, a giant supercontinent that included parts of today's Africa, India, Madagascar, Australia and Antarctica. The heat and pressure from those collisions bent and stretched the rocks in this area, almost like warm clay.

Some researchers think another patch of anorthosite about 60 kilometers to the north was once joined to Saririaky. They suggest the original rock was pulled apart into two pieces as the land around it shifted.

Studying Moon-like rocks on Earth can also help scientists learn more about how the Moon formed and changed over time.
why_it_matters: Rocks on Earth that match the Moon's surface let scientists study lunar history without leaving the planet. The site also records how ancient continents collided.

background_read: Astronauts on the International Space Station orbit Earth and often take photos of interesting places on the ground below.
Rocks are grouped by how they form, and igneous rocks form when melted rock cools, either on the surface or deep underground.
Earth's continents slowly move, and long ago some of them crashed together to form a giant supercontinent called Gondwana.
Because the Moon's bright highlands are made of anorthosite, studying the same rock on Earth helps scientists understand the Moon.
